column3: Whether the team learns from each sprint and shows it.
column6: The team explains, with named examples, what worked, what did not, and what it would do differently, and the handoff reflects it.
column9: The team names general lessons with few specifics; the handoff does not show them.
column12: No lessons the team can articulate.

column3: Whether the team has written down what it is building, in terms the partner agreed to.
column6: Requirements are complete, prioritized, and current; what shipped matches them, or the difference was negotiated with the partner.
column9: Requirements are mostly documented; there is drift between the document and what shipped.
column12: Requirements are missing or stale; the delivered work does not map to them.

column3: Whether working software exists, advances, and can be run by someone other than the team.
column6: The software is deployed where it needs to run, documented for its successor, and used by the partner or their users, and no gap the partner raised remains open.
column9: The software is deployed and functional, with gaps the team has named and not yet closed.
column12: Not deployed, or deployed but unusable without the team present.

column3: Who ran the software, on one ladder for every project. Where the Definition of Shipped records a custom scale, the partner scores on it instead, from half to all of the points.
column5: People outside the team depend on it (full points)
column6: For example, the partner's staff run it in their daily operations; a release of the open-source project includes the team's contributions; someone who didn't build it, such as a graduate student in the lab or a peer, reproduced the team's result from the published artifact without the team's help; people outside the team keep using it on their own (tens of heavy or hundreds of light users).
column8: Someone outside the team runs it in their own environment (90% of the points)
column9: For example, the partner is integrating it into production; the open-source project merged the team's contributions; someone outside the team reran the pipeline on real data and got the team's numbers; two dozen people outside the team used it, not friends or classmates asked as a favor.
column11: An outsider ran it and the team acted on what they found (80% of the points)
column12: For example, the partner's feedback on a prototype is addressed in a newer version; maintainers reviewed a PR and the team revised it; the partner's group ran it on real data and the team fixed what they found; a dozen people outside the team used it, not friends or classmates asked as a favor, or a user study ran to completion.
column14: An outsider ran it once (70% of the points)
column15: For example, the partner tried a prototype; a PR is open in the open-source project; the partner ran it once on real data, on the team's setup; friends tried a deployed build.
column17: The partner watched it run on their real inputs (60% of the points)
column18: The partner saw a live demo or a recording, but nobody outside the team has operated it.
column20: Nobody outside the team has run it (half the points)

column3: Whether the whole team shows up, any member can answer for the project, and the work is visibly shared.
column6: The whole team attends, prepared; anyone can speak to the project; disagreements are resolved and reported to the partner; work is visibly spread across members.
column9: Most members attend most meetings; one or two members carry the meetings; disagreements show in a meeting and are settled by the next one.
column12: Members miss meetings without notice; one person does the talking and the work; conflict shows and nobody manages it.

column3: Whether the partner always knows where the project stands without asking.
column6: Every meeting has an agenda beforehand, hears from every student, and ends with notes afterward; demos show working software, and updates arrive on the agreed schedule.
column9: Most meetings have an agenda before and notes after; one or two students rarely speak; the partner occasionally has to chase an update.
column12: Meetings have no agenda or notes; the same one or two people speak; the partner chases for updates; demos are slides instead of running software.
